e-8879.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface of Revolution: Rotation About the x-Axis
e-8879.problem: The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(x,\theta)$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=x^2$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in \left[0, 1\right].$ What is $\mathbf{r}?$
e-8879.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in[a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x) = x^2 \geq 0$ for all $x \in \left[0,1\right].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \big\langle x, \: x^2 \cos\theta, \: x^2\sin\theta \big\rangle,
\quad
x \in \left[0, 1\right],
\quad
\theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

e-8880.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface of Revolution: Rotation About the y-Axis or z-Axis
e-8880.problem: The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(y,\theta)$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=1-\cos{y}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis for $y \in [0, \pi].$ What is $\mathbf{r}?$
e-8880.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y) = 1-\cos{y} \geq 0$ for all $y \in [0, \pi].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\mathbf{r}(y,\theta) = 
\big\langle (1-\cos{y}) \cos\theta, \: 
y, \: 
(1-\cos{y}) \sin\theta 
\big\rangle,
\quad
y \in[0, \pi],
\quad
\theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

e-12364.knowledge_point: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution
e-12364.problem:
The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=e^{x/2}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in [0,2]$ is given by

$$
\big\langle \text{_______}\,, \:-e^{x/2} \cos\theta, \: -e^{x/2}\sin\theta \big\rangle.
$$

What is the $1$st component of the product?
e-12364.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=e^{x/2} \geq 0$ for all $x \in [0,2].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=e^{x/2},$ and 

$$
D = \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=e^{x/2},$ we obtain $f' = \dfrac12 e^{x/2}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x},\,-{e}^{x/2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{e}^{x/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $1$st component of the product is $\dfrac{1}{2}e^x.$

e-12365.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to find an integral expression for the surface area generated when the curve $x=\sin z$ is rotated by $2\pi$ radians about the $z$-axis for $z \in [0, \pi].$
e-12365.worked_solution:
Notice that $x=\sin z \geq 0$ for all $z \in [0, \pi].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\sin z,$ and

$$
D = \big\{ (z,\theta) \, : \, 0 \leq z \leq \pi , \, 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\big\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=\sin z,$ we obtain $f'(z) = \cos z.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡z\sqrt{1+(\operatorname{cos}⁡z)^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡z\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=1+cot⁡x by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[π4,3π4]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨x,π(1+cot⁡x)2sin⁡θ,π(1+cot⁡x)2cos⁡θ⟩
b
⟨2π(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ,2π(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,x⟩
c
⟨x,(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ⟩
d
⟨(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ,x⟩
e
⟨x,2π(1+cot⁡x)2cos⁡θ,2π(1+cot⁡x)2sin⁡θ⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Rotation about the x-axis preserves x and traces a circle in the yz-plane with radius 1+cot(x). Thus r(x,θ)=⟨x,(1+cot(x))cos(θ),(1+cot(x))sin(θ)⟩ for θ∈[0,2π), which is option c.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: The vector-valued function $r(x,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4}].$ Which of the following could be $r?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x\ge 0$ for all $x\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4}].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,(1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4}],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 1
?

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=1+cot⁡x by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[π4,3π4]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨x,π(1+cot⁡x)2sin⁡θ,π(1+cot⁡x)2cos⁡θ⟩
b
⟨2π(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ,2π(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,x⟩
c
⟨x,(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ⟩
d
⟨(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ,x⟩
e
⟨x,2π(1+cot⁡x)2cos⁡θ,2π(1+cot⁡x)2sin⁡θ⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A point (x,y,z) on the surface generated by rotating the graph of y=f(x) by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[a,b] has the position vector

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[a,b],θ∈[0,2π).

First, notice that y=f(x)=1+cot⁡x≥0 for all x∈[π4,3π4].

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r(x,θ)=⟨x,(1+cot⁡x)cos⁡θ,(1+cot⁡x)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[π4,3π4],θ∈[0,2π).

content.problem: The vector-valued function $r(x,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4}].$ Which of the following could be $r?$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x\ge 0$ for all $x\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4}].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,(1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(1+\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4}],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 3
?

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=1−x2 by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[−1,1]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨1−x2cos⁡θ,1−x2sin⁡θ,x⟩
b
⟨1−x2sin⁡θ,1−x2cos⁡θ,x⟩
c
⟨x,1−x2csc⁡θ,1−x2sec⁡θ⟩
d
⟨x,1−x2cos⁡θ,1−x2sin⁡θ⟩
e
⟨x,1−x2sin⁡θ,1−x2cos⁡θ⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Rotation about the x-axis directly gives ⟨x,√(1−x²)cos(θ),√(1−x²)sin(θ)⟩, option d. Its coordinates satisfy x²+y²+z²=1 and cover the entire sphere. Option e also parametrizes this surface by exchanging sine and cosine; options a and b also cover the same sphere because of its symmetry.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: The vector-valued function $r(x,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [-1,1].$ Which of the following could be $r?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [-1,1].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [-1,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 3
?

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=1−x2 by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[−1,1]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨1−x2cos⁡θ,1−x2sin⁡θ,x⟩
b
⟨1−x2sin⁡θ,1−x2cos⁡θ,x⟩
c
⟨x,1−x2csc⁡θ,1−x2sec⁡θ⟩
d
⟨x,1−x2cos⁡θ,1−x2sin⁡θ⟩
e
⟨x,1−x2sin⁡θ,1−x2cos⁡θ⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A point (x,y,z) on the surface generated by rotating the graph of y=f(x) by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[a,b] has the position vector

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[a,b],θ∈[0,2π).

First, notice that y=f(x)=1−x2≥0 for all x∈[−1,1].

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r(x,θ)=⟨x,1−x2cos⁡θ,1−x2sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[−1,1],θ∈[0,2π).

content.problem: The vector-valued function $r(x,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [-1,1].$ Which of the following could be $r?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [-1,1].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [-1,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.html:
Question 4
?

r(x,θ)=⟨x,_______,(4x2−x4)sin⁡θ⟩

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=4x2−x4 by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[−2,2]. What is the second component of r?

a
4x2cos⁡θ
b
πx4sin⁡θ
c
2π(4x2−x4)cos⁡θ
d
(2x−x2)sin⁡θ
e
(4x2−x4)cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A point (x,y,z) on the surface generated by rotating the graph of y=f(x) by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[a,b] has the position vector

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[a,b],θ∈[0,2π).

First, notice that y=f(x)=4x2−x4≥0 for all x∈[−2,2].

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r(x,θ)=⟨x,(4x2−x4)cos⁡θ,(4x2−x4)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[−2,2],θ∈[0,2π).

Therefore, the second component of r is (4x2−x4)cos⁡θ.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the second component is f(x)cos(θ)=(4x²−x⁴)cos(θ), option e. The incorrect feedback applies to the deliberately submitted option d.

content.problem:
$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,\text{_______},\,(4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(x,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [-2,2].$ What is the second component of $r?$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [-2,2].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,(4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,(4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [-2,2],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

  

Therefore, the second component of $r$ is $(4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

before.html:
Question 5
?

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=ln⁡(x−1) by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[2,5]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨ln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ,x⟩
b
⟨2πln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ,2πln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,x⟩
c
⟨x,ln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ⟩
d
⟨x,πln2⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ,πln2⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ⟩
e
⟨x,ln2⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln2⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Rotation about the x-axis preserves x and traces a circle of radius ln(x−1) in the yz-plane. Thus r(x,θ)=⟨x,ln(x−1)cos(θ),ln(x−1)sin(θ)⟩ for x∈[2,5] and θ∈[0,2π), which is option c.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: The vector-valued function $r(x,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [2,5].$ Which of the following could be $r?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\ge 0$ for all $x\in [2,5].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [2,5],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

The vector-valued function r(x,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=ln⁡(x−1) by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[2,5]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨ln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ,x⟩
b
⟨2πln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ,2πln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,x⟩
c
⟨x,ln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ⟩
d
⟨x,πln2⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ,πln2⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ⟩
e
⟨x,ln2⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln2⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A point (x,y,z) on the surface generated by rotating the graph of y=f(x) by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[a,b] has the position vector

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[a,b],θ∈[0,2π).

First, notice that y=f(x)=ln⁡(x−1)≥0 for all x∈[2,5].

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r(x,θ)=⟨x,ln⁡(x−1)cos⁡θ,ln⁡(x−1)sin⁡θ⟩,x∈[2,5],θ∈[0,2π).

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/56a380b075d10862170ed9c9a45c07dddff3eaef1ea9fb3109a61cc3d27b5ac4.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\ge 0$ for all $x\in [2,5].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [2,5],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨\text{_______},\,y,\,({y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(y,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={y}^{3}-{y}^{4}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [0,1].$ What is the first component of $r?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

  

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y)={y}^{3}-{y}^{4}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,1].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨({y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,({y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

  

Therefore, the first component of $r$ is $({y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

$$

$$

$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y)=\operatorname{csc}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{2}].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is  

$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨\operatorname{csc}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{2}],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

  

Therefore, the first component of $r$ is $\operatorname{csc}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y)=\operatorname{csc}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{2}].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is  

$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨\operatorname{csc}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{2}],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

  

Therefore, the first component of $r$ is $\operatorname{csc}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

before.html:
Question 8
?

r(z,θ)=⟨__________,(2z−1)cos⁡θ,z⟩

The vector-valued function r(z,θ) above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=2z−1 by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[0,2]. What is the first component of r?

a
(2z−1)sin⁡θ
b
sin⁡θ
c
2zsin⁡θ
d
z
e
zsin⁡θ
Submit

decision.explanation: Rotation about the z-axis preserves z and traces a circle of radius 2^z−1 in the xy-plane. Since the second component is (2^z−1)cos(θ), the first can be (2^z−1)sin(θ), option a.

r(z,θ)=⟨__________,(2z−1)cos⁡θ,z⟩

The vector-valued function r(z,θ) above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=2z−1 by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[0,2]. What is the first component of r?

a
(2z−1)sin⁡θ
b
sin⁡θ
c
2zsin⁡θ
d
z
e
zsin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A point (x,y,z) on the surface generated by rotating the graph of y=f(z) by 2π radians about the z-axis has the position vector

r=⟨f(z)sin⁡θ,f(z)cos⁡θ,z⟩,z∈[a,b],θ∈[0,2π).

First, notice that y=f(z)=2z−1≥0 for all z∈[0,2].

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r(z,θ)=⟨(2z−1)sin⁡θ,(2z−1)cos⁡θ,z⟩,z∈[0,2],θ∈[0,2π).

Therefore, the first component of r is (2z−1)sin⁡θ.

before.html:
Question 9
?

The vector-valued function r(y,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve x=sin2⁡y by 2π radians about the y-axis for y∈[0,π]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨y,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ,cos2⁡ycos⁡θ⟩
b
⟨sin2⁡ycos⁡θ,y,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩
c
⟨y,sin2⁡ycos⁡θ,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩
d
⟨sin2⁡ysin⁡θ,2πy,cos2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩
e
⟨sin2⁡ysin⁡θ,y,cos2⁡ycos⁡θ⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Rotation about the y-axis preserves y and traces circles in the xz-plane with radius sin²(y). Thus r(y,θ)=⟨sin²(y)cos(θ),y,sin²(y)sin(θ)⟩, which is option b.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: The vector-valued function $r(y,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={sin}^{2}⁡y$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [0,\pi ].$ Which of the following could be $r?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y)={sin}^{2}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,\pi ].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨{sin}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,{sin}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [0,\pi ],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

The vector-valued function r(y,θ) parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve x=sin2⁡y by 2π radians about the y-axis for y∈[0,π]. Which of the following could be r?

a
⟨y,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ,cos2⁡ycos⁡θ⟩
b
⟨sin2⁡ycos⁡θ,y,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩
c
⟨y,sin2⁡ycos⁡θ,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩
d
⟨sin2⁡ysin⁡θ,2πy,cos2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩
e
⟨sin2⁡ysin⁡θ,y,cos2⁡ycos⁡θ⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A point (x,y,z) on the surface generated by rotating the graph of x=f(y) by 2π radians about the y-axis has the position vector

r=⟨f(y)cos⁡θ,y,f(y)sin⁡θ⟩,y∈[a,b],θ=[0,2π).

First, notice that x=f(y)=sin2⁡y≥0 for all y∈[0,π].

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r(y,θ)=⟨sin2⁡ycos⁡θ,y,sin2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩,y∈[0,π],θ∈[0,2π).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option b: rotation about the y-axis preserves y and gives x=sin²(y)cos(θ), z=sin²(y)sin(θ). These trace circles of radius sin²(y). The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface of Revolution: Rotation About the y-Axis or z-Axis
content.problem: The vector-valued function $r(y,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={sin}^{2}⁡y$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [0,\pi ].$ Which of the following could be $r?$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y)={sin}^{2}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,\pi ].$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨{sin}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,{sin}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [0,\pi ],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

after.problem:
$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{__________},\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(z,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y={e}^{1-{z}^{2}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [0,1].$ What is the second component of $r?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071875/assets/04de4ea7dc617be1429c596812ce4f450c2cdaafd8d94d86f75e68a6743acba9.png)

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(z)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(z)={e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [0,1].$  

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is  

$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [0,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Therefore, the second component of $r$ is ${e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
⟨\text{_______}\,,\,-\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ and 

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le \pi /4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}={sec}^{2}⁡x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x,\,-\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=tan⁡x by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[0,π4] is given above. What is the 1st component of the product?

a
sin⁡xcos2⁡x
b
cos2⁡x
c
2cot⁡x
d
sec2⁡x
e
tan⁡xsec2⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that y=tan⁡x≥0 for all x∈[0,π4]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,(x,θ)∈D

where f(x)=tan⁡x, and

D={(x,θ):0≤x≤π/4,0≤θ<2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rx′=⟨∂x∂x,∂y∂x,∂z∂x⟩=⟨1,f′cos⁡θ,f′sin⁡θ⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨0,−fsin⁡θ,fcos⁡θ⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

rx′×rθ′=|ijk1f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ0−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|=⟨|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|,−|1f′sin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|,|1f′cos⁡θ0−fsin⁡θ|⟩=⟨ff′cos2⁡θ+ff′sin2⁡θ,−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ⟩=⟨ff′,−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ⟩.

Since f=tan⁡x, we obtain f′=sec2⁡x. So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

rx′×rθ′=⟨tan⁡xsec2⁡x,−tan⁡xcos⁡θ,−tan⁡xsin⁡θ⟩.

after.problem:
$$
⟨\text{_______}\,,\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y={x}^{2}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,1]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $y={x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)={x}^{2},$ and 

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f={x}^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨2{x}^{3},\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,(x,θ)∈D

where f(x)=x2, and

D={(x,θ):0≤x≤1,0≤θ<2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rx′=⟨∂x∂x,∂y∂x,∂z∂x⟩=⟨1,f′cos⁡θ,f′sin⁡θ⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨0,−fsin⁡θ,fcos⁡θ⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

rx′×rθ′=|ijk1f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ0−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|=⟨|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|,−|1f′sin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|,|1f′cos⁡θ0−fsin⁡θ|⟩=⟨ff′cos2⁡θ+ff′sin2⁡θ,−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ⟩=⟨ff′,−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ⟩.

Since f=x2, we obtain f′=2x. So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

rx′×rθ′=⟨2x3,−x2cos⁡θ,−x2sin⁡θ⟩.

Your Answer:
x2−2x

⟨−e1−z2cos⁡θ,−e1−z2sin⁡θ,_______⟩

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve x=e1−z2 by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[0,1] is given above. What is the 3rd component of the product?

a
2ze1−z2
b
z(e1−z2)2
c
(e1−z2)2
d
−2ze2(1−z2)
e
1e1−z2
Submit

decision.explanation: Using r(z,θ)=⟨f(z)cos(θ),f(z)sin(θ),z⟩ gives r_z×r_θ=⟨−f cos(θ),−f sin(θ),ff′⟩. Here f=e^(1−z²) and f′=−2ze^(1−z²), so the third component is −2ze^(2(1−z²)), option d.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
$$
⟨\,-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,,\,-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,,\,\text{_______}⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={e}^{1-{z}^{2}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [0,1]$ is given above. What is the $3$rd component of the product?
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)={e}^{1-{z}^{2}},$ and    

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since $f={e}^{1-{z}^{2}},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=-2z{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is    

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,-2z{e}^{2(1-{z}^{2})}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

⟨−e1−z2cos⁡θ,−e1−z2sin⁡θ,_______⟩

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve x=e1−z2 by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[0,1] is given above. What is the 3rd component of the product?

a
2ze1−z2
b
z(e1−z2)2
c
(e1−z2)2
d
−2ze2(1−z2)
e
1e1−z2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that x=e1−z2≥0 for all z∈[0,1]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨f(z)cos⁡θ,f(z)sin⁡θ,z⟩,(z,θ)∈D

where f(z)=e1−z2, and

D={(z,θ):0≤z≤1,0≤θ<2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rz′=⟨∂x∂z,∂y∂z,∂z∂z⟩=⟨f′cos⁡θ,f′sin⁡θ,1⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨−fsin⁡θ,fcos⁡θ,0⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

rz′×rθ′=|ijkf′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ1−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ0|=⟨|f′sin⁡θ1fcos⁡θ0|,−|f′cos⁡θ1−fsin⁡θ0|,|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|⟩=⟨−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ,f′fcos2⁡θ+f′fsin2⁡θ⟩=⟨−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ,f′f⟩.

Since f=e1−z2, we obtain f′=−2ze1−z2. So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

rz′×rθ′=⟨−e1−z2cos⁡θ,−e1−z2sin⁡θ,−2ze2(1−z2)⟩.

$$
⟨\,-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,,\,-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,,\,\text{_______}⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={e}^{1-{z}^{2}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [0,1]$ is given above. What is the $3$rd component of the product?
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)={e}^{1-{z}^{2}},$ and    

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since $f={e}^{1-{z}^{2}},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=-2z{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is    

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{e}^{1-{z}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,-2z{e}^{2(1-{z}^{2})}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
$$
⟨\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{y}},\text{_______}\,,\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{y}}⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [1,4]$ is given above. What is the $2$nd component of the product?
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [1,4].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}},$ and  

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

 

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y},\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{y}},\,\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}},\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{y}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

⟨cos2⁡ycos⁡θ,_______,cos2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve x=cos2⁡y by 2π radians about the y-axis for y∈[−π2,π2] is given above. What is the 2nd component of the product?

a
2sin⁡ycos3⁡y
b
−sin⁡ycos2⁡y
c
 −sin⁡2ycos⁡y
d
 sin⁡2y
e
−sin2⁡2y
Submit

decision.explanation: For rotation about the y-axis, the second component of r_y×r_θ is −ff′. Here f(y)=cos²(y) and f′(y)=−2sin(y)cos(y), so −ff′=2sin(y)cos³(y), option a.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
⟨\,{cos}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\text{_______}\,,\,{cos}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={cos}^{2}⁡y$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}]$ is given above. What is the $2$nd  component of the product?
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={cos}^{2}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)={cos}^{2}⁡y,$ and  

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y},\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f={cos}^{2}⁡y,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨{cos}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡y{cos}^{3}⁡y,\,{cos}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15

⟨cos2⁡ycos⁡θ,_______,cos2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve x=cos2⁡y by 2π radians about the y-axis for y∈[−π2,π2] is given above. What is the 2nd component of the product?

a
2sin⁡ycos3⁡y
b
−sin⁡ycos2⁡y
c
 −sin⁡2ycos⁡y
d
 sin⁡2y
e
−sin2⁡2y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that x=cos2⁡y≥0 for all y∈[−π2,π2]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨f(y)cos⁡θ,y,f(y)sin⁡θ⟩,(y,θ)∈D

where f(y)=cos2⁡y, and

D={(y,θ):−π2≤y≤π2,0≤θ<2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ry′=⟨∂x∂y,∂y∂y,∂z∂y⟩=⟨f′cos⁡θ,1,f′sin⁡θ⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨−fsin⁡θ,0,fcos⁡θ⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

ry′×rθ′=|ijkf′cos⁡θ1f′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|=⟨|1f′sin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|,−|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|,|f′cos⁡θ1−fsin⁡θ0|⟩=⟨fcos⁡θ,−f′fcos2⁡θ−f′fsin2⁡θ,fsin⁡θ⟩=⟨fcos⁡θ,−f′f,fsin⁡θ⟩.

Since f=cos2⁡y, we obtain f′=−2sin⁡ycos⁡y. So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

ry′×rθ′=⟨cos2⁡ycos⁡θ,2sin⁡ycos3⁡y,cos2⁡ysin⁡θ⟩.

history.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={cos}^{2}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)={cos}^{2}⁡y,$ and  

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y},\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f={cos}^{2}⁡y,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨{cos}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡y{cos}^{3}⁡y,\,{cos}^{2}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve y=xx+1 is rotated by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[0,4].

a
2π∫04xx+11+1(x+1)4dx
b
2π∫041x+11+x(x+1)2dx
c
2π∫041(x+1)41+xx+1dx
d
2π∫04xx+11+1(x+1)2dx
e
2π∫041(x+1)21+xx+1dx
Submit

decision.explanation: With f(x)=x/(x+1), f′(x)=1/(x+1)². The parametrization r=⟨x,f cos(θ),f sin(θ)⟩ gives r_x×r_θ=⟨ff′,−f cos(θ),−f sin(θ)⟩, whose magnitude is f√(1+(f′)²). Integrating θ over [0,2π] yields option a.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y=\frac{x}{x+1}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,4].$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=\frac{x}{x+1}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,4].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1},$ and

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f{f}^{′})^{2}+(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{x+1}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{x+1}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(x+1)^{4}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve y=xx+1 is rotated by 2π radians about the x-axis for x∈[0,4].

a
2π∫04xx+11+1(x+1)4dx
b
2π∫041x+11+x(x+1)2dx
c
2π∫041(x+1)41+xx+1dx
d
2π∫04xx+11+1(x+1)2dx
e
2π∫041(x+1)21+xx+1dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that y=xx+1≥0 for all x∈[0,4]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨x,f(x)cos⁡θ,f(x)sin⁡θ⟩,(x,θ)∈D

where f(x)=xx+1, and

D={(x,θ):0≤x≤4,0≤θ≤2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rx′=⟨∂x∂x,∂y∂x,∂z∂x⟩=⟨1,f′cos⁡θ,f′sin⁡θ⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨0,−fsin⁡θ,fcos⁡θ⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

rx′×rθ′=|ijk1f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ0−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|=⟨|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|,−|1f′sin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|,|1f′cos⁡θ0−fsin⁡θ|⟩=⟨ff′cos2⁡θ+ff′sin2⁡θ,−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ⟩=⟨ff′,−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ⟩

and

‖rx′×rθ′‖=(ff′)2+(−fcos⁡θ)2+(−fsin⁡θ)2=f2(f′)2+f2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=f2(f′)2+f2=f1+(f′)2.

Therefore, the surface area is

A=∬SdS=∬D‖rx′×rθ′‖dxdθ=∬Df1+(f′)2dxdθ=∫04f1+(f′)2∫02πdθdx=∫04f1+(f′)2⋅θ|02πdx=2π∫04f1+(f′)2dx.

Since f(x)=xx+1, we obtain f′(x)=1(x+1)2. So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

2π∫04f1+(f′)2dx=2π∫04xx+11+(1(x+1)2)2dx=2π∫04xx+11+1(x+1)4dx.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Surface of Revolution
content.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y=\frac{x}{x+1}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,4].$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=\frac{x}{x+1}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,4].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1},$ and

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f{f}^{′})^{2}+(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{x+1}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{x+1}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(x+1)^{4}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x)=\frac{x}{x+1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{x+1}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{x+1}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(x+1)^{4}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Set f(y)=1+y² and r(y,θ)=⟨f(y)cos(θ),y,f(y)sin(θ)⟩. Then r_y×r_θ=⟨f cos(θ),−ff′,f sin(θ)⟩ has magnitude f√(1+(f′)²)=(1+y²)√(1+4y²). Integrating θ from 0 to 2π gives option d.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $x=1+{y}^{2}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [-1,1].$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $x=1+{y}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=1+{y}^{2},$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=1+{y}^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2y.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 17
?

Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve x=1+y2 is rotated by 2π radians about the y-axis for y∈[−1,1].

a
∫−11(1+y2)1+4y2dy
b
2π∫−111+4y2dy
c
∫−11(1+y2)1+y2dy
d
2π∫−11(1+y2)1+4y2dy
e
2π∫−11(1+y2)1+y2dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that x=1+y2≥0 for all y∈[−1,1]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨f(y)cos⁡θ,y,f(y)sin⁡θ⟩,(y,θ)∈D

where f(y)=1+y2, and

D={(y,θ):−1≤y≤1,0≤θ≤2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ry′=⟨∂x∂y,∂y∂y∂z∂y⟩=⟨f′cos⁡θ,1,f′sin⁡θ⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨−fsin⁡θ,0,fcos⁡θ⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

ry′×rθ′=|ijkf′cos⁡θ1f′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|=⟨|1f′sin⁡θ0fcos⁡θ|,−|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|,|f′cos⁡θ1−fsin⁡θ0|⟩=⟨fcos⁡θ,−ff′cos2⁡θ−ff′sin2⁡θ,fsin⁡θ⟩=⟨fcos⁡θ,−ff′,fsin⁡θ⟩

and

‖ry′×rθ′‖=(fcos⁡θ)2+(−ff′)2+(fsin⁡θ)2=f2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)+f2(f′)2=f2+f2(f′)2=f1+(f′)2.

Therefore, the surface area is

Since f=1+y2, we obtain f′=2y. So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Surface of Revolution
content.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $x=1+{y}^{2}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [-1,1].$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $x=1+{y}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=1+{y}^{2},$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=1+{y}^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2y.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 18
?

Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve y=1z2 is rotated by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[1,5].

a
2π∫151z21+4z6dz
b
2π∫151z41+4z6dz
c
2π∫151z41−1z3dz
d
2π∫151z21+2z3dz
e
2π∫151z41+2z3dz
Submit

decision.explanation: Let f(z)=1/z² and r(z,θ)=⟨f(z)sin(θ),f(z)cos(θ),z⟩. The fundamental vector product has magnitude f(z)√(1+(f′(z))²). Since f′(z)=−2/z³, integrating over a full rotation gives 2π∫₁⁵(1/z²)√(1+4/z⁶) dz, option a.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,5].$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,5].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}},$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,1\le z\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(z)=-\frac{2}{{z}^{3}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{2}{{z}^{3}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{{z}^{6}}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve y=1z2 is rotated by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[1,5].

a
2π∫151z21+4z6dz
b
2π∫151z41+4z6dz
c
2π∫151z41−1z3dz
d
2π∫151z21+2z3dz
e
2π∫151z41+2z3dz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that y=1z2≥0 for all z∈[1,5]. The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

r=⟨f(z)cos⁡θ,f(z)sin⁡θ,z⟩,(z,θ)∈D

where f(z)=1z2, and

D={(z,θ):1≤z≤5,0≤θ≤2π}.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rz′=⟨∂x∂z,∂y∂z,∂z∂z⟩=⟨f′cos⁡θ,f′sin⁡θ,1⟩rθ′=⟨∂x∂θ,∂y∂θ,∂z∂θ⟩=⟨−fsin⁡θ,f(y)cos⁡θ,0⟩

Next, the fundamental vector product is

rz′×rθ′=|ijkf′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ1−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ0|=⟨|f′sin⁡θ1fcos⁡θ0|,−|f′cos⁡θ1−fsin⁡θ0|,|f′cos⁡θf′sin⁡θ−fsin⁡θfcos⁡θ|⟩=⟨−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ,f′fcos2⁡θ+f′fsin2⁡θ⟩=⟨−fcos⁡θ,−fsin⁡θ,f′f⟩.

and

‖rz′×rθ′‖=(−fcos⁡θ)2+(−fsin⁡θ)2+(f′f)2=f2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)+f2(f′)2=f2+f2(f′)2=f1+(f′)2.

Therefore, the surface area is

A=∬SdS=∬D‖rz′×rθ′‖dzdθ=∬Df1+(f′)2dzdθ=∫15f1+(f′)2∫02πdθdz=∫15f1+(f′)2⋅θ|02πdz=2π∫15f1+(f′)2dz.

Since f(z)=1z2, we obtain f′(z)=−2z3. So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

2π∫15f1+(f′)2dz=2π∫151z21+(−2z3)2dz=2π∫151z21+4z6dz.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Surface of Revolution
content.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,5].$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,5].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}},$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,1\le z\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(z)=-\frac{2}{{z}^{3}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{2}{{z}^{3}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{{z}^{6}}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{2}},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(z)=-\frac{2}{{z}^{3}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{2}{{z}^{3}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{{z}^{6}}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: For r(x,θ)=⟨x,x⁴cos(θ),x⁴sin(θ)⟩, the fundamental vector product is ⟨4x⁷,−x⁴cos(θ),−x⁴sin(θ)⟩. Its magnitude is x⁴√(1+16x⁶). Integrating over θ∈[0,2π] and x∈[−2,2] gives option a.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y={x}^{4}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [-2,2].$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $y={x}^{4}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [-2,2].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)={x}^{4},$ and

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f{f}^{′})^{2}+(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f={x}^{4},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=4{x}^{3}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{4}\sqrt{1+(4{x}^{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{4}\sqrt{1+16{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
